mechanism.rule: Energy Conservation Program for Appliance Standards: Certification Requirements, Labeling Requirements, and Enforcement Provisions for Certain Consumer Products and Commercial Equipment (final rule, 10 CFR Parts 429 and 431)
mechanism.agency: Department of Energy (Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy)
mechanism.required: <cite index="11-1">DOE published a final rule to establish and amend the certification provisions, labeling requirements, and enforcement provisions for specific consumer products and commercial and industrial equipment.</cite> <cite index="15-10">The products named include central air conditioners and heat pumps, dishwashers, residential clothes washers, pool heaters, dehumidifiers, external power supplies, battery chargers, computer room air conditioners and direct-expansion outdoor air systems, among others.</cite> The obligations fall on the manufacturers who certify these products to DOE. The rule changed reporting, labeling and enforcement provisions.
mechanism.benefits: The portions of DOE's document that were reviewed do not state a quantified dollar or energy-savings benefit for this rule. Ballotpedia, a secondary source, lists the estimated benefit as $0 and says the rule was <cite index="17-3">not deemed significant</cite>. DOE's full regulatory-review sections were not opened to confirm there is no quantified benefit elsewhere in the document. DOE's stated qualitative benefit is that <cite index="15-9">certification reports give DOE and consumers current efficiency information and support effective enforcement.</cite>
mechanism.costs: Ballotpedia, a secondary source, reports an estimated cost of $212,065. How that figure is built up was not confirmed. No CBO, GAO or court finding disputing these estimates was found.
mechanism.agency_reasons: DOE said it was establishing and amending certification requirements, labeling requirements, and enforcement provisions for these products and equipment to ensure reporting that is consistent with currently applicable energy conservation standards and test procedures.
mechanism.sponsor_reasons: A James Magazine item reproducing Rep. Andrew Clyde's (R-GA) statement describes the rule as one that <cite index="42-2">put additional costs and red tape on appliance manufacturers, with consumers bearing the ultimate cost.</cite> That wording appears in the magazine's narration, not inside Clyde's quoted statement. A House Republican release carrying statements from Clyde and Rep. McClain described the rule as placing <cite index="39-10">undue burdens on manufacturers and consumers, leading to increased costs and limiting consumer choice.</cite> That release described the rule as requiring higher energy efficiency standards. Democratic floor statements were not reviewed in full.
mechanism.status: Became law. H.J.Res.42 passed the House on 2025-03-05. The Senate passed the resolution 2025-04-30 (52-46); <cite index="58-1">the Senate Daily Press logged the vote as party line.</cite> <cite index="20-4">It was sent to the President on May 6, 2025, and signed May 9, 2025, becoming Pub. L. 119-8.</cite> <cite index="22-8,22-9,22-10">The law states that Congress disapproves the rule (89 Fed. Reg. 81994, October 9, 2024) and that it shall have no force or effect.</cite> The rule is therefore void and not in force.

outcomes.claim: DOE removed the 2024 certification, labeling and enforcement provisions from 10 CFR parts 429 and 431. DOE said it was acting because Pub. L. 119-8, pursuant to the Congressional Review Act (CRA), <cite index="20-6">disapproved and caused DOE's October 9, 2024 final rule to have no force or effect</cite>. DOE also said the action <cite index="54-6">relieves manufacturers from certain certification, compliance, and enforcement requirements.</cite> <cite index="55-3">The removal rule took effect September 9, 2025.</cite> The reporting changes the 2024 rule had added no longer apply to manufacturers of the covered products.

outcomes.counterpoint: The sources record no changes in actual enforcement or compliance.

outcomes.claim: DOE found no measurable change in reporting burden or hours for residential clothes washers from these amendments. DOE's own estimates of reporting burden for the rule's other products, including electric pool heaters, are in section IV.C of the final rule, which could not be read, so they are not stated here. Any burden figures would be DOE's forecasts, not measured outcomes.

outcomes.quote: DOE makes a final determination that these amendments would not cause any measurable change in reporting burden or hours for RCWs.
outcomes.counterpoint: DOE stated that certification reports provide DOE and consumers with efficiency information and support effective enforcement. That information benefit is not quantified in the sources opened, so no dollar comparison with the burden can be made.

outcomes.claim: An efficiency-advocacy group (ASAP) said the nullified requirements concerned certification only. It said they did not affect the efficiency levels products must meet, calling the fight over them <cite index="60-5">mostly a sideshow.</cite> ASAP also said the resolution would make it more difficult for DOE or other parties to identify products that do not comply with standards. This is advocacy-group analysis, not an official estimate.

notes: (1) I read the Federal Register rule only in excerpts: the synopsis, the Paperwork Reduction Act figures and the regulatory-review headings. I did not read DOE's full cost-benefit discussion. No quantified benefit was found, and Ballotpedia's $0 benefit figure is a secondary source. (2) The five paperwork-cost line items sum exactly to Ballotpedia's $212,065. I did not map each line to a product, and the full-text cost totals should be checked against the rule PDF before publication. (3) The House Republican release describes the rule as requiring products to meet higher efficiency standards. The CRS summary and ASAP describe it as changing certification, labeling and enforcement provisions and aligning reporting with existing standards. I treated the CRS and Federal Register descriptions as authoritative on what the rule did. (4) No CBO or GAO analysis of this resolution and no court finding on DOE's estimates were found. (5) I found no credible record of what happened to appliance prices, energy use, compliance rates or DOE enforcement counts after nullification, and that absence is itself the finding. (6) This is a sibling of other CRA resolutions on DOE efficiency standards (for example H.J.Res.75 on commercial refrigeration standards). Those change efficiency levels, but this one does not, so their analyses should not be conflated. (7) DOE's 2025 removal rule cited good cause to skip notice and comment because it implements Pub. L. 119-8. I did not retrieve its own burden-reduction figures.
